Chapter 1: When Belief Replaces Reason in Public Life
Picture this: a group of friends huddled around a kitchen table, swapping stories deep into the night. One of them brings up how certain ideas are everywhere— in the news, in every conversation, even in classrooms. And these aren’t just opinions anymore. They’re treated almost like sacred truths, totally off-limits for questioning.
That’s when you realize— for so many people, politics isn’t just about policies. It’s become something closer to faith.
This is the world we see when we really stop and look at how modern liberalism shapes American life. The line between honest debate and unquestioned belief gets blurry, especially in places where big decisions get made— like schools, courts, and the media. The folks who steer these institutions often say they’re guided by logic and facts. But if you look closer, their choices reveal something deeper: a real devotion to a worldview that’s almost immune to challenge. Almost like a new kind of religion.
Think about a classroom, where a teacher— determined to keep any trace of traditional faith out of the lesson— carefully edits the curriculum. Anything that might hint at religion is scrubbed away. The teacher might see this as neutrality, but what actually happens? The absence of faith-based ideas doesn’t leave empty space. Instead, it gets filled by a new orthodoxy— one that treats secular liberalism as the only lens that matters.
And this shift isn’t just about what gets taught. It’s about how. Imagine a parent, frustrated after a school board meeting, wondering why their concerns get brushed aside so quickly. The officials answer with a kind of ironclad certainty— not open-mindedness, but more of a dogmatic response. The parent walks away with that uneasy feeling: that questioning this prevailing view isn’t just discouraged— it’s almost heresy.
You’ll see the same thing in the media. News anchors and commentators deliver their takes with total authority, rarely admitting the assumptions behind their arguments. And when someone dares to challenge the story everyone else is telling? The pushback is fast and fierce. Suddenly, there are accusations— of ignorance, bigotry, or worse. The message rings out loud and clear: dissent isn’t just wrong. It’s dangerous.
Over time, it adds up. People start to notice: the ones who claim to be defending reason are often the most unwilling to have a real debate. The language of science and progress? It’s used to close doors, not open them. Before long, you end up with a culture where certain beliefs can’t be touched— and anyone who asks the hard questions gets pushed out.
That’s really the heart of it: today’s liberalism has taken on the weight and shape of a secular faith. Its followers might say they’ve left religion behind, but in practice? They’ve built their own set of sacred beliefs, rituals, and even heresies. Only now, it’s not churches that enforce the rules— it’s the schools, the courts, and the media. And anyone who dares to question this new orthodoxy feels the consequences.
So, how did we get here? This isn’t just about politics. It’s about something deeply human— our need for meaning, for belonging, for certainty. When traditional faith is pushed out of public life, something else always rushes in to fill the gap. For many, that “something” is the dogma of liberalism— dressed up as reason, but lived with all the passion and certainty of religion.
